challenges.name: token-cookie-quiz
challenges.title: Which flag protects against what?
challenges.description: Two pieces of evidence from the review of the AI-written login helper: a refresh cookie with HttpOnly and SameSite but a parent Domain, and an access token moved from localStorage into a cookie while an XSS bug is still open.

questions.question:
A first fix of the AI's helper, response of POST https://api.codedev.test/auth/login:

Set-Cookie: refresh_token=rt_Q2xh...; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict; Domain=codedev.test; Path=/; Max-Age=1209600

The community forum runs third-party software on https://forum.codedev.test. A learner opens a forum thread from a link on https://app.codedev.test.

Statement: "Because the cookie is HttpOnly and SameSite=Strict, the browser does not send refresh_token to forum.codedev.test."
questions.explanation: False. SameSite is about the site that starts the request, and a site is the registrable domain: app.codedev.test, api.codedev.test and forum.codedev.test are all the same site, codedev.test. HttpOnly only hides the cookie from document.cookie. Which hosts receive the cookie is decided by Domain: Domain=codedev.test sends it to every subdomain, so the forum software, its logs and anyone who controls it see the refresh token. The fix is to drop Domain (a host-only cookie for api.codedev.test) and to narrow Path to /auth/refresh. The misconception is that SameSite separates subdomains.

questions.question: Before the fix, the SPA did: localStorage.setItem("access_token", body.accessToken); fetch(url, { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${localStorage.getItem("access_token")}` } }); After the fix, the access token is only in Set-Cookie: __Host-cd_at=eyJhbGci...; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/; Max-Age=900 and the SPA calls fetch(url, { credentials: "include" }). A course comment still renders unescaped HTML, so this payload runs on app.codedev.test: Statement: "After the fix the payload can no longer read the access token, but while the page is open it can still send authenticated requests to the API, for example fetch('https://api.codedev.test/me/email', { method: 'PUT', credentials: 'include', ... })."
questions.explanation: True. HttpOnly keeps the token out of document.cookie and the token is no longer in localStorage, so the payload cannot copy it to evil.example and replay it later from anywhere. But the script runs inside app.codedev.test, a same-site origin the API trusts with credentials, so the browser attaches the cookie to its requests just as it does for the real SPA. HttpOnly limits XSS to acting during the victim's session; it does not stop XSS. Escaping output and a Content Security Policy are what stop the script from running. The misconception is that HttpOnly cookies make XSS harmless.

challenges.name: spot-the-ai-mistake-token-cookie
challenges.title: Spot the AI Mistake: a token cookie JavaScript can read
challenges.description: The request sent to an AI coding assistant was: "Set the auth cookies after login so the frontend can show the user's name." It wrote buildLoginResponse for POST https://api.codedev.test/auth/login and changed the SPA to keep body.accessToken in localStorage. Login works, the header says "Hi, Lan Nguyen", refresh works, and the pull request was merged. A security review then found that a script on app.codedev.test can read both tokens and that the forum on forum.codedev.test receives the refresh token. Fix buildLoginResponse so it meets the review's list: (1) the body is only { user: { id, displayName } }, no token; (2) the access token is in the cookie __Host-cd_at: hidden from scripts, Secure, sent only to api.codedev.test (every path), SameSite=Lax, Max-Age 900; (3) the refresh token is in the cookie __Secure-cd_rt: hidden from scripts, Secure, sent only to https://api.codedev.test/auth/refresh, SameSite=Strict, Max-Age 1209600; (4) display_name is not sensitive and stays readable by the SPA on app.codedev.test with Domain=codedev.test, Path=/, Secure, SameSite=Lax and Max-Age 1209600, its value encoded with encodeURIComponent. The test runner contains a small browser with the RFC 6265 rules for Domain and Path and the cookie prefix rules (a __Host- or __Secure- cookie that breaks them is rejected), the SPA, and a fake API that accepts the access token as a Bearer header or a cookie. Input: { sessions: [{ user, tokens }], probes: [...] }; the output lists, per learner, the login, then each probe: API calls, stored cookies and their attributes, what a script on app.codedev.test can read, the login body, and the cookies sent to the forum and to an ordinary API path. The public tests pass on the AI's code; the hidden tests check the flags, Path, Domain and prefix rules, the body, and that display_name stays readable. Up to 120 learners per test.
hints: For each value the response hands to the browser, ask two questions: who can read it (scripts on app.codedev.test, the forum, only the API) and who needs to read it. Which of the three values does the SPA itself actually need?

Look at the shared attribute string the assistant reused for both cookies, and at the last property of the response body. A Domain attribute makes a cookie go to every subdomain; leaving it out makes it host-only. Then check the prefix rules: __Host- allows only Path=/ and no Domain, __Secure- only requires Secure.

A similar case on another endpoint: an instructor-preview cookie that only https://api.codedev.test/preview should receive would be `preview_grant=...; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict; Path=/preview; Max-Age=600` with no Domain, while a theme cookie the SPA reads on every subdomain would be `theme=dark; Domain=codedev.test; Path=/; Secure; SameSite=Lax`. Only values that are safe to show to any script may skip HttpOnly.
